nodes.label: English-to-Spanish Cognate Suffix-Conversion System ('Magic Key' mnemonic)
nodes.rationale: Madrigal's book's central pedagogical device: ~19 productive English-to-Spanish suffix-conversion rules (-tion to -cion, -ty to -dad, -ist to -ista, -ous to -oso, etc.) taught as generative rules rather than item-by-item vocabulary — the single mechanism most directly relevant to later mechanics-analysis of productive word-formation.
nodes.norm_label: english-to-spanish cognate suffix-conversion system ('magic key' mnemonic)

nodes.label: Diminutive Suffixation (-ito/-ico/-illo) as Affective Register Marker
nodes.rationale: A productive bound-morpheme system marking both literal smallness and, independently, affection/endearment; explicitly regionally split (-ico favored in north Spain, -illo in south Spain, -ito strongly preferred in Latin America) — a cross-linguistically common source of register-shifted vocabulary worth tracking for later slang-mechanics synthesis.
nodes.norm_label: diminutive suffixation (-ito/-ico/-illo) as affective register marker

nodes.label: Grammatical Double Negation
nodes.rationale: Unlike English, standard Spanish requires every negatable element in a negative sentence to itself be negated (no vi nada, no vi a nadie) — presented across sources as correct grammar, not a stigmatized construction, worth flagging since English-speaking slang analysis sometimes wrongly treats double negation as inherently substandard.
nodes.norm_label: grammatical double negation

nodes.label: Gustar-type Reverse-Subject Construction
nodes.rationale: The 'to please' construction where the liked thing is grammatically the subject and the liker takes an indirect object pronoun (me gusta la musica); word order before/after the verb carries statement-vs-question semantic weight; encantar works identically for a stronger 'to love' sense.
nodes.norm_label: gustar-type reverse-subject construction

nodes.label: Body-Part/Animal Metaphor as Idiom-Formation Mechanism
nodes.rationale: A rich case set of Spanish colloquial idioms built through concrete-to-abstract figurative extension from a literal body-part or animal image (donkey's ear for foolishness, hands in dough for being caught red-handed, an eleven-yard shirt for over-committing, a wild beast for fury; also lengua larga 'long tongue' for a gossip) — a word-formation mechanism distinct from affixation, catalogued at scale in both Madrigal's Part 2 idiom appendix and PMP Advanced Grammar's Unit 12.
nodes.norm_label: body-part/animal metaphor as idiom-formation mechanism

nodes.label: Learning Spanish Like Crazy, Level I (whole course)
nodes.rationale: Unifying concept node for the single Level I course (32 lessons + 2 insult supplements + readme) split across 4 extraction files, per the dispatch's instruction to treat split source material as one book/course.
nodes.norm_label: learning spanish like crazy, level i (whole course)

nodes.label: Madrigal's Magic Key to Spanish (whole book)
nodes.rationale: Unifying concept node for the single 740-page book split across 3 extraction files (part1, part2, glossary appendix) per the dispatch's explicit instruction that all Madrigal's files are one book, not three.
nodes.norm_label: madrigal's magic key to spanish (whole book)

nodes.label: Direct/Indirect Object Pronoun System (lo/la/le, leismo, double-object stacking)
nodes.rationale: Covers the lo/la vs le 'to/for' acid test, the le/lo leismo dialectal split (PMP Advanced), and the double-object-pronoun stacking system with the se-for-le/les substitution rule (drilled in Learning Spanish Like Crazy Lecciones 28-29).
nodes.norm_label: direct/indirect object pronoun system (lo/la/le, leismo, double-object stacking)

nodes.label: Personal 'a' (human direct-object marker)
nodes.rationale: The untranslatable preposition 'a' obligatorily inserted before a human direct object (Invite a Roberto); taught across multiple sources as a fixed attachment to specific high-frequency verbs rather than a fully general rule.
nodes.norm_label: personal 'a' (human direct-object marker)

nodes.label: Reflexive Verb System (physical action + 'to get + adjective')
nodes.rationale: Spanish's much heavier reliance on reflexive verbs than English, split between literal body-directed actions (banarse, lavarse) and a productive 'to get + adjective' pattern (casarse, cansarse, enfermarse, emborracharse) each transparently derived from a related non-reflexive root.
nodes.norm_label: reflexive verb system (physical action + 'to get + adjective')

nodes.label: Spanish Taboo/Insult Register Vocabulary

nodes.norm_label: spanish taboo/insult register vocabulary

nodes.label: Voseo (vos/sos pronoun-and-conjugation paradigm)
nodes.rationale: FLAGSHIP FIND per the extraction checklist: a fully worked, distinct second-person pronoun-and-conjugation system (vos instead of tu, with its own present indicative/imperative/subjunctive forms and the irregular ser-form 'sos') attested in Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay, Chile, and parts of Central America/southern Mexico — a genuine parallel grammatical paradigm, not a lexical footnote.
nodes.norm_label: voseo (vos/sos pronoun-and-conjugation paradigm)
